title: JWT & OAuth 2.0: A Field Handbook for Tokens, Flows and Failures
summary: A dense study series on how bearer tokens actually work: JWT anatomy and signature verification, the OAuth 2.0 and OIDC flows worth using in 2026, refresh rotation, revocation strategies, and the mistakes that turn a token system into an auth bypass.

chapters.title: Tokens 101: Why Bearer Credentials Exist
points: Authentication answers 'who is this?'; authorization answers 'what may they do?' — JWT is a token format, OAuth 2.0 is an authorization framework, OIDC is authentication layered on OAuth
Bearer token definition (RFC 6750): whoever holds it can use it, no proof of possession — hence HTTPS-only and short lifetimes
Session cookies vs bearer tokens: server-side session = state in a store, lookup per request, instant revoke; bearer token = state carried by the client, no lookup, hard revoke
Stateless vs stateful trade-off: JWT trades a database read for a window of stale authorization until expiry
Opaque token vs structured (JWT) token: opaque is a random string meaningless to the client, validated by introspection; JWT is self-describing and locally verifiable
Where a token travels: `Authorization: Bearer eyJ...` header, never in a query string (leaks into access logs, Referer headers, browser history)
Example request/response pair showing a token issued at login and presented to a resource server
Vocabulary set used through the handbook: issuer, subject, audience, scope, claim, grant, principal
Rule of thumb: tokens for machine-to-machine and cross-domain APIs; plain server sessions are still correct for a single first-party web app

chapters.title: Anatomy of a JWT: Header, Payload, Signature
points: JWT = three base64url segments joined by dots: `header.payload.signature`; the signing input is the first two segments plus the dot, exactly as transmitted
base64url is encoding, not encryption — anyone can read a JWT payload; never put secrets, PII, or passwords in it
Header claims: `alg` (signing algorithm), `typ` (usually `JWT` or `at+jwt`), `kid` (key id for key lookup)
Registered claims: `iss`, `sub`, `aud`, `exp`, `nbf`, `iat`, `jti` — with what each is checked against
`exp`/`nbf`/`iat` are NumericDate: seconds since epoch, not milliseconds — a 1000x error makes tokens valid for 50,000 years
Private/custom claims: `scope` (space-delimited string), `roles`, `email`, tenant id — and why claim bloat hurts (header size limits ~8KB at proxies)
Worked decode of a real token: raw string, decoded header JSON, decoded payload JSON, signature bytes
JWS (signed, the common case) vs JWE (encrypted, payload hidden) — a 'JWT' in the wild almost always means JWS Compact Serialization
Compact vs JSON serialization; why the compact form is what fits in a header
Mistake: treating an unverified decode as authentication — decoding and verifying are separate operations in every library

chapters.title: Signatures and Keys: HS256, RS256, ES256, JWKS
points: HMAC family (HS256/384/512): one shared secret both signs and verifies — every verifier can also forge tokens
RSA family (RS256/PS256) and ECDSA (ES256): private key signs at the issuer, public key verifies anywhere — the right choice when verifiers are third parties
EdDSA/Ed25519 as the modern compact option; ES256 signatures ~64 bytes vs RS256 ~256 bytes
Comparison row set: algorithm | key type | token size | verifier can forge? | typical use
JWKS: the issuer publishes public keys at `/.well-known/jwks.json`, discovered via `/.well-known/openid-configuration`; each key has a `kid`
Verification flow: read `kid` from header, fetch matching JWK (cached), verify signature, then check claims — cache the JWKS with a TTL and refetch on unknown `kid`
Key rotation: publish the new key before signing with it, keep the old key in JWKS until the longest-lived token expires
HMAC secret strength: at least 256 bits of entropy; a dictionary-word secret on HS256 is brute-forceable offline from a single captured token
Mistake: allowing the token's own `alg` header to pick the verification algorithm — pin the expected algorithm(s) server-side
Mistake: `alg: none` accepted, and the RS256→HS256 confusion attack where the public key is used as an HMAC secret

chapters.title: Verifying a Token Correctly: The Full Checklist
points: Ordered validation steps: parse → pin `alg` → resolve key by `kid` → verify signature → validate `iss` → validate `aud` → check `exp`/`nbf` → check `scope`/`roles` → optional `jti` replay check
`iss` must equal the exact expected issuer string, compared byte-for-byte, not merely 'contains'
`aud` must contain this API's identifier; a token minted for another API of the same issuer must be rejected
Clock skew: allow a small leeway (30–60s) on `exp`/`nbf`, never an unbounded one; leeway is not a substitute for time sync
Code example: verification with pinned algorithms, expected issuer and audience, and explicit failure handling
Distinguish 401 (token missing/invalid/expired) from 403 (valid token, insufficient scope) — with `WWW-Authenticate: Bearer error="invalid_token"`
Never trust `sub` as a display name or email; `sub` is an opaque issuer-scoped identifier and can be non-unique across issuers
Authorization is still your job: a valid token proves identity, not that this user owns resource #42 — check ownership at the data layer
Mistake: verifying signature but skipping `aud`, letting a token from a low-trust service unlock a high-trust one
Mistake: catching all verification exceptions and falling back to an anonymous-but-allowed path

chapters.title: OAuth 2.0 Roles, Endpoints and the Consent Model
points: Four roles: resource owner (the user), client (the app), authorization server (issues tokens), resource server (the API)
Why OAuth exists: delegated access without sharing the password — the 'valet key' model
Endpoints: `/authorize` (front channel, browser redirect), `/token` (back channel, direct POST), `/introspect`, `/revoke`, `/userinfo`, `/jwks.json`
Front channel vs back channel: the front channel is visible to the user and browser (never put secrets there), the back channel is server-to-server over TLS
Client types: confidential (can keep a secret — server-side apps) vs public (SPAs, mobile, CLIs — no secret possible)
Scopes are coarse permissions requested by the client and consented to by the user; the AS may issue fewer scopes than requested (downscoping)
`redirect_uri` must be pre-registered and matched exactly by the AS — no wildcards, no prefix matching
`state` parameter carries CSRF protection; `nonce` binds an OIDC id_token to the request
Example `/authorize` URL with every parameter labelled: response_type, client_id, redirect_uri, scope, state, code_challenge
Mistake: treating scopes as roles — scopes limit what the client may ask for, not what the user is allowed to do

chapters.title: Authorization Code + PKCE: The Flow You Should Use
points: Step sequence: client builds code_verifier → derives code_challenge → redirect to `/authorize` → user authenticates and consents → AS redirects back with `code` + `state` → client POSTs code + code_verifier to `/token` → receives access + refresh (+ id) token
PKCE (RFC 7636): `code_verifier` is 43–128 random chars, `code_challenge = BASE64URL(SHA256(verifier))` with `code_challenge_method=S256`
What PKCE defends against: authorization code interception on mobile custom URL schemes and in the browser — the stolen code is useless without the verifier
PKCE is now recommended for confidential clients too, not just public ones (OAuth 2.1 makes it mandatory)
Authorization codes are single-use and short-lived (~30–60s); the AS should revoke the whole grant if a code is replayed
`state` verification on return is mandatory and separate from PKCE — PKCE stops code theft, `state` stops CSRF/login-fixation
Diagram: the six-hop dance across user agent, client backend and authorization server, with front/back channel marked
Full worked example: the `/authorize` request, the redirect back, and the `/token` POST body with `grant_type=authorization_code`
Mistake: skipping `state` validation, or generating `state`/`verifier` with `Math.random()` instead of a CSPRNG
Mistake: storing the code_verifier somewhere a different tab or origin can read it

chapters.title: The Other Grants: Client Credentials, Device Code, and the Dead Ones
points: Client credentials grant: machine-to-machine, no user present, `grant_type=client_credentials` with client_id/secret or mTLS/private_key_jwt — never issues a refresh token

Device authorization grant (RFC 8628): input-constrained devices (TVs, CLIs) — user_code shown on device, user visits verification_uri, client polls `/token` honoring `slow_down` and `authorization_pending`
Refresh token grant as its own `grant_type=refresh_token` call
Implicit flow (`response_type=token`): deprecated — tokens land in the URL fragment, leak via history and Referer, no refresh possible
Resource Owner Password Credentials (ROPC): deprecated — the client sees the password, defeats the point of OAuth, breaks MFA and federation
OAuth 2.1 summary of changes: PKCE required, implicit and ROPC removed, exact redirect URI matching, refresh tokens must be sender-constrained or rotated
Token exchange (RFC 8693) for service-to-service delegation and downscoping an incoming token
Comparison table: grant | user present? | client type | refresh token? | status in 2026
Decision guide: SPA/mobile → code+PKCE; server app → code+PKCE with secret; cron/service → client credentials; smart TV → device code
Mistake: reaching for ROPC to 'simplify' a first-party login, then being unable to add MFA or SSO later

chapters.title: OIDC: id_token vs access_token
points: OpenID Connect adds an identity layer: request `scope=openid`, receive an `id_token` alongside the access token
id_token is always a JWT for the client to consume, proving who logged in; access_token is for the API and may be opaque
Never send an id_token to an API as a bearer credential, and never let an API accept one — wrong audience, wrong purpose
id_token claims: `iss`, `sub`, `aud` (= client_id), `exp`, `iat`, `nonce`, `auth_time`, `acr`/`amr`
`nonce` validation: the client generates it, the AS echoes it into the id_token, the client compares — blocks token replay/injection
`/userinfo` endpoint for profile claims that are too large or too volatile for the id_token
Discovery document `/.well-known/openid-configuration`: endpoints, supported algorithms, supported scopes
Comparison table: id_token vs access_token vs refresh_token — audience, format, lifetime, who validates it, where it may be stored
Example decoded id_token with each claim annotated
Mistake: using `email` from an id_token as a primary key when the issuer allows email changes or doesn't verify it (`email_verified`)

chapters.title: Refresh Tokens, Rotation and Reuse Detection
points: Why refresh exists: short access tokens (5–15 min) limit damage; the refresh token (days–months) buys new ones without re-prompting the user
Refresh tokens are always used on the back channel with client authentication where possible; they are long-lived, so they are the crown jewels
Rotation: every refresh call returns a NEW refresh token and invalidates the old one — a one-time-use chain
Reuse detection: if an already-used refresh token is presented, the whole token family is revoked, because it means one copy was stolen
Sliding vs absolute expiry: sliding extends on use, absolute caps total session length — production systems usually set both
Sender-constrained tokens: DPoP (RFC 9449) proof-of-possession headers and mTLS-bound tokens turn a bearer token into a non-bearer one
Concurrency hazard: two parallel requests both refresh, the second gets a reuse error and logs the user out — fix with a single-flight mutex/leader tab and a small grace window
Diagram: happy-path rotation chain vs a stolen-token branch triggering family revocation
Example refresh request/response with the rotated token highlighted
Mistake: issuing refresh tokens to a client_credentials client, or handing a refresh token to browser JavaScript instead of an HttpOnly cookie / BFF

chapters.title: Revocation: The Hard Part of Stateless Auth
points: The core problem: a signed JWT is valid until `exp` — there is no built-in 'log out everywhere' or 'this user is now fired'
`/revoke` (RFC 7009) kills a refresh token immediately; already-issued access tokens keep working until they expire
Introspection (RFC 7662): the resource server asks the AS 'is this token still active?' — accurate but adds a network hop per request, cacheable for seconds
Denylist by `jti` or by `sub` + `iat` cutoff in Redis, with entries expiring at the token's own `exp` so the list stays small
Short access-token lifetime is the real revocation mechanism: 5-minute tokens mean a 5-minute worst-case exposure window
Backchannel logout and front-channel logout in OIDC for propagating sign-out to relying parties
Comparison table: strategy | revocation latency | per-request cost | operational complexity
Password change, role downgrade and account deletion should all bump a per-user token-validity epoch checked at verification
Trade-off framing: stateless speed vs immediate revocation is a dial, not a binary — hybrid (short JWT + refresh introspection) is the common answer
Mistake: 'logout' that only deletes the token client-side while the server still honors it

chapters.title: Where to Put the Token: Browser Storage and Its Attacks
points: localStorage/sessionStorage: readable by any JS on the origin — one XSS and every token is exfiltrated; no automatic CSRF risk
HttpOnly + Secure + SameSite cookies: invisible to JS, but sent automatically, so CSRF protection is required
SameSite values: `Lax` (default, blocks most cross-site POSTs), `Strict`, `None` (requires Secure, needed for true cross-site APIs)
CSRF defenses that pair with cookies: double-submit token, Origin/Sec-Fetch-Site header checks, custom-header requirement on state-changing calls
BFF (Backend-for-Frontend) pattern: the browser holds only a session cookie, the server holds the tokens — the recommended shape for SPAs today
In-memory storage for access tokens plus a cookie-held refresh token as the middle-ground pattern; page reload costs a silent refresh
Mobile/native: iOS Keychain and Android Keystore, plus system browser (ASWebAuthenticationSession / Custom Tabs) instead of an embedded WebView
Comparison table: storage | XSS-safe? | CSRF-safe? | survives reload? | complexity
Never log tokens: scrub `Authorization` headers from request logs, APM traces and error reports
Mistake: putting a JWT in a URL for a download link or email, where it lands in server logs and browser history forever

chapters.title: The Mistake Museum: How Token Systems Get Broken
points: `alg: none` accepted, or the algorithm read from the attacker-controlled header instead of pinned server-side
RS256→HS256 confusion: the public key is fed to an HMAC verifier as the secret, so anyone can mint tokens
Signature never verified — the app just base64-decodes the payload and trusts `role: admin`
Missing `aud`/`iss` checks, letting a token minted for a different tenant or a different service be replayed
Weak or committed HMAC secret ('secret', 'changeme'), or the same secret across staging and production
`exp` in milliseconds, or no `exp` at all — a token that never dies
Open redirect on `redirect_uri` via wildcard/prefix matching, letting an attacker capture the authorization code
Missing `state`/`nonce` validation enabling CSRF login-fixation and id_token injection
Trusting client-supplied claims: scopes, roles, tenant or price copied from the token payload without server-side authority
Authorization code not single-use; refresh token not rotated; logout that revokes nothing
Ignoring the `kid` header and trying every key, or fetching a key from an attacker-controlled `jku`/`x5u` URL
Debug endpoints that echo decoded tokens, and error messages that leak whether a user exists

chapters.title: Putting It Together: A Reference Architecture
points: End-to-end picture: SPA → BFF → authorization server → API gateway → microservices, showing which component holds which token
Recommended defaults: authorization code + PKCE, RS256 or ES256 with JWKS, 10-minute access tokens, rotating refresh tokens, HttpOnly cookies
Gateway verifies the signature once and forwards trusted identity headers; internal services still verify audience for defense in depth
Service-to-service calls use client credentials or token exchange, never the user's own access token forwarded blindly
Observability: log `jti`, `sub`, `iss` and token age (never the token itself); alert on refresh-reuse detections and signature-failure spikes
Migration path from server sessions to tokens, and the dual-validation window it requires
Testing checklist: expired token, wrong audience, wrong issuer, tampered payload, `alg: none`, replayed code, reused refresh token
Sizing and cost: token size vs header limits, JWKS cache hit rate, introspection QPS budget
Decision summary of the trade-offs made across the handbook: statelessness vs revocation, lifetime vs UX, JWT vs opaque

chapters.title: JWT & OAuth Cheatsheet
points: JWT layout: `base64url(header).base64url(payload).base64url(signature)`; signing input is `header.payload`
Claim quick-reference: `iss` issuer, `sub` subject, `aud` audience, `exp` expiry, `nbf` not-before, `iat` issued-at, `jti` token id, `scope` permissions
Algorithm picker: HS256 for a single trusted service, RS256/ES256 when third parties verify, EdDSA for compact modern stacks, never `none`
Grant picker: SPA/mobile → code+PKCE; server app → code+PKCE; service → client credentials; TV/CLI → device code; implicit & ROPC → never
Validation order: pin alg → resolve kid → verify signature → iss → aud → exp/nbf → scope → replay check
Lifetime defaults: access 5–15 min, refresh 7–30 days rotating, id_token minutes, auth code 30–60s single-use
Endpoint map: `/authorize`, `/token`, `/introspect`, `/revoke`, `/userinfo`, `/.well-known/openid-configuration`, `/.well-known/jwks.json`
Storage picker: BFF cookie (best) > HttpOnly cookie + CSRF defense > in-memory access token > localStorage (avoid)
Status codes: 401 invalid/expired token, 403 valid token but insufficient scope, plus `WWW-Authenticate: Bearer`
Spec index: RFC 6749 OAuth 2.0, 6750 bearer, 7009 revocation, 7519 JWT, 7636 PKCE, 7662 introspection, 8628 device, 8693 exchange, 9449 DPoP, OAuth 2.1 draft
Ten-item pre-ship audit: alg pinned, aud checked, iss checked, exp enforced, secret strong, redirect_uri exact, state+nonce validated, code single-use, refresh rotating, tokens never logged
